For the purpose of this judgment, the facts of the present case shall suffice.

3. Briefly, the facts, which are germane for deciding these Constitutional Petitions are that the Petitioners are taxpayers registered under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“Ordinance, 2001”). The Directorate General, Intelligence and Investigation Inland Revenue (“DG, I&I”) initiated the proceedings against the Petitioners, invoking the provisions contained in Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (“AMLA”), read with relevant provisions of Ordinance, 2001. As per the case of the respondent department, the Petitioners were issued notices and after grant of opportunities of hearing for rendering explanation qua the alleged conduct, the FIRs have been registered against the Petitioners in terms of the provisions contained in AMLA on the basis of alleged predicate offences, followed by issuance of notices/summons and initiation of consequential proceedings.

4. It is in this backdrop that the Petitioners have sought to invoke the Constitutional Jurisdiction of this Court, essentially questioning the assumption and exercise of jurisdiction under AMLA, registration of the FIRs and consequential proceedings, inter alia, on the premise that the underlying tax liability had not first been determined through the adjudicatory mechanism provided under the Ordinance, 2001; some of the Petitioners have argued that in their respective cases the tax determination has already been made by the assessing officer(s) and the matter having been culminated in favour of the Petitioners upto the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (“Tribunal”), therefore, no case is made out against them. Others have argued that the determination of the tax liability against the Petitioners is a sine qua non for initiating the proceedings of such a nature, as enunciated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the case of Taj International ,therefore, the proceedings under AMLA are patently without jurisdiction. In one of the connected petitions, vires/legal validity of Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation-FBR, through Director and others v. Taj International (Pvt.) Ltd. and others (PLD 2025 SC 633=2025 PTD 1270)

W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 5 Notification No.SRO 425(I)/2016 dated 14.05.2016, whereby certain offences under the Ordinance, 2001 were included in Schedule-I to AMLA, has also been called in question on the grounds of competence and legality of the said SRO.

5. In a nub, the challenge brought about through these Constitutional Petitions is rooted in the threshold submissions of “due process” and “fair trial” as envisaged in Articles 4 & 10A of the Constitution.
6. Learned counsel for the Petitioners, in substance, raise the following common grounds:

a. contend that the proceedings initiated under AMLA cannot commence merely on the basis of allegations concerning the tax matters without determining the related tax liability, if any, under the regular adjudicatory regime spelt out by virtue of the provisions contained in the Ordinance, 2001, which determination may then form basis for questioning that as to whether an offence has been committed;

b. argue that the Ordinance, 2001 provides a complete mechanism for inquiry, assessment, appeal and recovery, therefore, the initiation of criminal proceedings without or during the pendency of such process of law, amounts to frustrating the statutory scheme and leading to infringement of fundamental rights of due process and fair trial;

c. add that in absence of determination of the alleged predicate offence and identification of ‘proceeds of crime’, the essential ingredients for invocation of the provisions contained in AMLA are not attracted, consequently, the registration of the Impugned FIRs followed by notices/summons are without lawful authority and jurisdiction.

d. It has been forcefully argued that the statutory scheme of AMLA does make ‘proceeds of crime’ central to the offence of money laundering, while defining a predicate offence by W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 6 reference to the Schedule, therefore, an overwhelming reliance has been placed upon the principles enunciated in Taj International, to contend that criminal prosecution founded upon alleged tax evasion cannot precede the requisite adjudication/determination under the fiscal laws.

e. Another ground common in substance is that the respondent authorities cannot bypass the proceedings contemplated under the Ordinance, 2001 and thus, cannot resort to criminal machinery for establishing and proving the commission of an offence without there being a final determination of a tax liability, which is either still uncertain or has concluded in favour of the taxpayer.

f. While referring to the provisions contained in Section 110D of the Ordinance, 2001, it is contended that clause (c) of subsection (6) of Section 100D of the Ordinance, 2001 excludes the offences under the Ordinance, 2001 in the circumstances contemplated therein; therefore, invocation of Sections 192, 192A and 199 of the Ordinance, 2001 for setting up a case of predicate offences by resorting to the provisions contained in AMLA, is without jurisdiction.

g. Further submits that proceedings concerning the Petitioners' tax affairs were already pending before the officer exercising regular jurisdiction under the Ordinance, 2001 when the Directorate I&I intervened and initiated parallel criminal proceedings, therefore, the impugned FIRs, notices and summons amount to bypassing the statutory proceedings already underway.

h. Plead that SRO No.425(I)/2016 dated 14.05.2016, whereby offences under sections 192, 192A, 194 and 199 of the Ordinance, 2001 were inserted in Schedule-I to AMLA, has not validly been issued by the Federal Government and is contrary W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 7 to the law laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of M/s. Mustafa Impex.

i. further submit that an Investigating Officer under AMLA neither has any lawful authority to assume jurisdiction as couched in Sections 111 or 122 of the Ordinance, 2001 as the impugned notices issued by the respondents have all the trappings of a notice or order under the aforesaid provisions, which is not the mandate of DG I&I nor the Investigation Officer can assess income or independently determine concealment or the amount of tax allegedly evaded as such a jurisdiction squarely falls within the domain of the competent authority under the Ordinance, 2001.

j. contend that proceedings under AMLA could not be set in motion merely on the basis of Suspicious Transaction Report (“STR”), its analysis by the Financial Monitoring Unit (“FMU”) and dissemination of the resultant information to the concerned investigating or prosecuting agency as these are automated desktop generated STR and the actions followed by those STRs, which cannot trump the question of basic liberties and due process, therefore, an Investigating Officer under AMLA could not lawfully register an FIR in respect of the predicate offences and the cognizance could only be taken upon a ‘complaint’ by the relevant officer, as contemplated by section 21 of AMLA, read with Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.P.C.”), as distinguished from a police report under Section 173 thereof.

l. In addition to above, there are certain factual variations qua the facts and circumstances of some of the Petitions whereby, the counsel for the petitioners have argued that the assessment proceedings initiated against the Petitioners by the revenue have been culminated upto the Tribunal in favour of the taxpayers/petitioners, therefore, unless those determinations so rendered under the taxation regime, as envisaged in the relevant statute i.e. Ordinance, 2001, are set aside, no FIR can be registered against such taxpayers/Petitioners.

m. With an intent to substantiate the submission viz the absence of due process in the impugned actions, it is argued that the due process has a wider scope than the concept of natural justice under the common law; the due process clause is an outstanding feature which has to be adhered to.

n. Shamim ur Rehman (PLD 1983 SC 457) W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. The reliance in this regard has further been placed upon the Supreme Court of Pakistan’s order dated 13.05.2026 passed in Crl.R.P. No.34/26 in Crl. No. 2928 of 2026. p. Since the petitioners have sought the relief of quashment of FIRs, therefore, during the course of hearing, learned counsel for the petitioners were specifically confronted viz the mandate and contours of jurisdiction exercised by this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution and the law laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan viz the questions of quashment of FIRs, learned counsel for the petitioners contend that since the respondents/investigating officers, who proceeded to register FIRs were doing an act of an investigation, performing the functions in connection with the affairs of the Federation, thus, they are amenable to the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199(1)(a)(ii) of the Constitution, therefore, this Court can declare such acts of the respondents to have been done without any lawful authority.

It is further argued that investigation can be corrected and necessary orders can be passed by this Court, if the aggrieved party alleges and proves that either the investigation has been initiated beyond jurisdiction of the investigation agency or the investigation has been initiated with mala fide intention, bad faith and in colorable exercise of power ; adds that the petitioners cannot be directed to resort to the provisions contained in Section 249-A or Section 265-K of the Cr.P.C. as the quashment is sought on the ground that the proceedings are ex facie without jurisdiction and continuation FIA through Director General FIA v. Syed Hamid Ali Shah (PLD 2023 SC 265) Messrs R.SIM and Co. Ltd. v. the District Magistrate (PLD 1966 SC 650), Ghulam Sarwar Zardari v. Piyar Ali alias Piyaro (2010 SCMR 624)

W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 11 of the same will constitute the abuse of process of Court , thus, as contended, the continuation of the proceedings would be a futile exercise and wastage of time, therefore, the FIRs may be quashed ; while placing reliance on the case of Abdul Aziz Menon , it is argued that the Supreme Court of Pakistan, while enunciating the law viz the powers exercised by the Chairman NAB under the provisions contained in National Accountability Ordinance, 1999 has held that even the opinion of the Chairman NAB is justiciable, therefore, the opinions formed in this case by the respondents for registration of cases is also justiciable; lastly contends in this regard that the instant case falls within the well-recognized exceptions to the legal rule of non-quashing of FIRs while exercising jurisdiction under Article 199 of the constitution as the ground of attack in this and connected cases is that the actions taken by the respondents are absolutely without lawful authority.

7. Conversely, learned counsel for the respondents, apart from laying a confrontal attack viz the maintainability of these Constitutional Petitions, have laid out the legislative background of the promulgation of AMLA and explained in great detail the process being followed by the Directorate of I&I, as couched in the applicable law, rules and SOPs framed; submit that proceedings under AMLA are independent of the assessment and recovery mechanism provided under the Ordinance, 2001; adds that the offence under Section 3 of AMLA is autonomous and by virtue of Explanation II thereto, conviction for the predicate offence is not a prerequisite of prosecution for money laundering as laundering stands on its own footing as a distinct criminal offence under Section 3 of AMLA; contends that the prior assessment or determination of tax liability under the Ordinance, 2001 is not a condition precedent for initiation of proceedings under AMLA; while placing reliance upon Section 39 of AMLA, it is contended that the special statutory regime created under AMLA, which is subsequent in time, has an Maritime Security Agency, Karachi v. Muhammad Saleem Khan (PLD 1994 SC 486) Muhammad Aslam (Amir Aslam) v. District Police Officer, Rawalpindi (2009 SCMR 141) Abdul Aziz Menon v. The State (PLD 2013 SC 594)

W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 12 overriding effect; submits that the DG I&I is not undertaking an exercise of assessment for recovery of tax and instead the investigation launched is confined to the question that whether the property/assets/funds in question constitutes the proceeds of crime and has thereafter been concealed, layered, possessed, transferred, converted or otherwise dealt with within the contemplation of Section 3 of AMLA.

8. The pursuit of the invocation of the Constitutional jurisdiction of this Court by filing these Petitions under Article 199 of the Constitution has been resisted on the ground that the questions concerning the source and character of funds, existence of proceeds of crime and acts allegedly constituting concealment, possession, layering or integration are disputed questions requiring evidence before the Court of competent jurisdiction i.e. the Special Court, therefore, considering the well settled law on the subject that this Court cannot embark upon to look into or determine the disputed questions of facts, the Constitutional Petitions in hand, as contended, are liable to be dismissed.

9. While further substantiating her submissions, learned counsel for the respondents contend that since AMLA itself contains statutory safeguards and remedies at different stages, including the requirement of reason to believe, confrontation of record and facts during investigation, proceedings concerning attachment and the remedy of appeal under section 23 of AMLA, therefore, as argued, these are the matters, which are required to be appreciated by the Court of competent jurisdiction and thus, does not furnish a basis for quashing the respective FIRs at the threshold.

10. It is contended that the special regime under Section 100D of the Ordinance, 2001 affords, subject to its conditions, immunity from the operation of Section 111 of the Ordinance, 2001 alone and does not constitute immunity from prosecution under AMLA; adds that the conditions attached to the concession, including genuine construction and investment through the prescribed banking channel, were not fulfilled and that the transactions relied upon involved fabricated completion certificates and circular transactions; contend that the statutory concession itself excludes W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 13 earnings from money laundering and, therefore, Section 100D of the Ordinance, 2001 cannot be invoked as a shield against proceedings under AMLA.

11. On the question of limitation, raised in some of the Constitutional Petitions viz the lapse of limitation for calling into question the assessments pertaining to the Tax Years in issue, learned counsel for the respondents not only disputes the factual premise by arguing that without prejudice to the fact that no limitation runs for taking cognizance of an offence being committed and the criminal prosecution can be launched when the occurrence of such an offence has surfaced, AMLA proceedings have commenced before the lapse of purported period of limitation; add that AMLA being a special statute does not contain corresponding limitation for initiation of such proceedings as the concealment, possession or disguise of alleged proceeds of crime constitutes continuing conduct and, therefore, the proceedings are not necessarily confined to the tax year in which the underlying transaction is alleged to have originated.
12. We have heard learned counsels for the parties at length and perused the available record with their able assistance.

13. Apart from the question of maintainability of this and connected Constitutional Petitions, the principal question laid for determination before us is whether the proceedings under AMLA, founded upon the alleged offences specified in the Ordinance, 2001 and being predicate offences in terms of the provisions read with the Schedule-I of AMLA can be initiated or continued without determination of the claimed corresponding tax liability under the Ordinance, 2001. The answer to this question indeed relates to and leads to the question of maintainability of these Constitutional Petitions. Petitioners’ arguments proceed substantially on the premise that the alleged accusations essentially relate to tax liability, therefore, without first determining the same under the Ordinance, 2001, there can be no predicate offence and consequently, no proceeds of crime capable of attracting AMLA. Having examined the statutory scheme and the law relied W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 14 upon by the parties, we are not persuaded to accept the proposition in such absolute terms for the following reasons:

14. Since the threshold submissions are rooted in the arguments advanced on the touchstone of due process, therefore, we deem it appropriate to deal this question ahead of all other questions. The historic origin of ‘Due Process of Law’ is usually traced back to Magna Carta – the Great Charter of 1215 where the basic idea underlined that phrase was expressed in its clause 29.

There is no cavil to the settled position of laws over the continents that “due process and procedural fairness go together, but it is not always clear whether they mean the same thing or what the differences between them are. The notion of due process has been associated with certain doctrines, both substantive and procedural, arising under American Constitution, while procedural fairness is more at home in the British context.

”10 The contours of ‘due process’ are not susceptible to any rigid or definite formulation. Whether the requirement of due process has been observed and adhered to is necessarily depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case, the nature of the proceedings involved and the statutory framework governing the same. What constitutes due process in a given case must consequently be examined in its own factual and legal setting rather than by application of an inflexible formula. ‘Procedural due process’ guarantees only that there is a fair decision making process before some action is taken directly impairing a person’s life, liberty or property. It is only necessary that a fair decision making process be used; the ultimate rule to be enforced need not to be fair and just, whereas, ‘substantive due process’ is concerned with the ability of the judiciary to review the substance of legislation. “By ‘substantive review’ we mean the judicial determination of the compatibility of the substance of law or executive action with the Constitution. The Court is concerned with the constitutionality of the underlying rule rather than with the fairness of the process by which the executive applies the rule to an individual. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 15 of review other than that involving procedural due process is a form of substantive review.”
Fazal Karim, J. has extensively quoted the Hurtado v.

California , whereby, Matthew J. proceeded to dismiss a contention of a prisoner, who claimed that his conviction and sentence were void on the ground that they were repugnant to the 14 th Amendment of the American Constitution; the contention was that it was essential to the due process of law to try him by a grand jury as known to the Common Law of England and as he had not been so tried, his conviction and sentence were void. While dismissing such a plea, it was held: “to what principle, then, are we to resort to ascertain whether this process, enacted by Congress, is due process? . . . . . The real syllabus of the passage quoted is that a process of law, which is not otherwise forbidden must be taken to be due process of law, if it can show the sanction of settled usage both in England and in this country; but it by no means follows that nothing else can be due process of law.”
To sum up, the following observations of Justice John Marshall Harlan II are relevant to the point in some abundance of clarity:

“Due process has not been reduced to any formula; its content cannot be determined by reference to any code. The best that can be said is that through the course of this Court’s decisions it has represented the balance which our Nation, built upon postulates of respect for the liberty of the individual, has struck between that liberty and the demands of organized society. If the supplying of content to this Constitutional concept has of necessity been a rational process, it certainly has not been one where judges have felt free to roam where unguided speculation might take them. The balance of which I speak is the balance struck by this country, having regard to what history teaches are the traditions from which it developed as well as the traditions from which it broke. That tradition is a living thing. A decision of this Court which radically departs from it could not long survive, while a decision which builds on what has survived is likely to be sound. No formula could serve as a substitute, in this area, for judgment and restraint.”

Page 16 Thus, the question that whether the element of ‘due process’ is offended by infringement of any constitutionally guaranteed rights of the Petitioners in these cases is a question which is dependent upon the facts of these cases, the applicable law of the land and rules/regulations framed thereunder, which are being elaborated herein below. Nonetheless, it is settled that due process is not what one contemplates to be the process to be followed, instead, it is the process, which is in adherence to the law of the land, as it stands when the law is applied.

15. At the outset, a distinction must be maintained between proceedings undertaken for assessment, determination and recovery of tax under the Ordinance, 2001 and criminal proceedings initiated under AMLA. The former determines the fiscal liability of a taxpayer, whereas, the latter investigates and prosecutes an offence created by a separate special enactment. Merely because the facts giving rise to a criminal prosecution may simultaneously entail civil or fiscal consequences does not denude the conduct of its criminal character. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Muhammad Ali’s case has reiterated that remedies arising under civil and criminal law may be pursued simultaneously though the two may overlap; they differ in their content and consequences and an act does not lose its criminal character merely because it has trappings of civil liability. Thus, pendency or availability of proceedings under the Ordinance, 2001 does not, by itself, exclude the operation of criminal proceedings initiated under a lawfully enacted and subsisting statute, where its ingredients are otherwise alleged to exist.

16. The legislative intent behind promulgation of AMLA is clear and unambiguous: that money laundering proceedings can be initiated, continued and concluded regardless of whether the scheduled offence has resulted in a conviction, in acquittal while the civil proceedings are still pending adjudication. The Scheme of AMLA envisages that while prior conviction is unnecessary, the prosecution is still required to prove a case beyond a reasonable doubt that the property/asset in question constitutes the ‘proceeds Muhammad Ali v. Samina Qasim Tarar and others (2022 SCMR 2001) W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 17 of crime’ derived from an unlawful predicate offence activity, therefore, the prosecution cannot secure an AMLA conviction purely on suspicions and all possible doubts will lead to the logical conclusion of case being dismissed. While initiating the proceedings on the basis of AMLA, as rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent, the prosecution not only runs a risk of dismissal of a criminal prosecution against the accused but also have to face the logical outcome of letting go the property/asset in question as clean property. Needless to observe that such consequence will flow from the stringent tests and standards of criminal prosecution where accused is law’s favourite child and all possible doubts shall go in his favour, wherever the link in the chain of prosecution’s case is broken.

17. The scheme of AMLA further fortifies the above conclusion. AMLA is a special and self-contained enactment designed to prevent money laundering and to provide for attachment and forfeiture of proceeds of crime. Clause (xxvi) of Section 2 defines a “predicate offence” by reference to the offences specified in Schedule-I; clause (xxviii) defines “proceeds of crime” as property derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, from the commission of a predicate offence; whereas clause (xxx) gives an expansive meaning to “property”, including cash and monetary instruments wherever located. Significantly, Section-XXII-A of Schedule-I, inter alia, include offences under Sections 192, 192A, 194 and 199 of the Ordinance, 2001, where the tax sought to be evaded is ten million rupees or more. Section 3 then creates the substantive offence of money laundering by encompassing acquisition, conversion, possession, use or transfer of property under clause (a); concealment or disguise of its true nature, origin, location, disposition, movement or ownership under clause (b); holding such property on behalf of another under clause (c); and participation in, association with, conspiracy to commit, attempt, aiding, abetting, facilitating or counseling the commission of such acts under clause (d), of course, subject to the statutory requirement of knowing or having reason to believe that the property constitutes proceeds of crime. Explanation-I to Section 3 permits such knowledge or reason to believe to be inferred from the factual circumstances, whereas Explanation- II expressly provides that, for proving an offence under Section 3, conviction W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 18 of an accused for the respective predicate offence shall not be required. The remaining provisions complete this special statutory framework: Section 4 prescribes punishment, fine and forfeiture of the property involved; Section 8 provides for attachment of property; Section 9 contemplates issuance of show-cause notice and an opportunity to the person concerned and, through sub-section (5), cessation of attachment upon acquittal; Section 21 makes the offence cognizable and provides for registration of an FIR; Section 23 provides a remedy of appeal against an order of attachment; while Section 39 gives AMLA overriding effect. A cumulative reading of these provisions, therefore, demonstrates that the legislature has not merely created the substantive offence of money laundering but has simultaneously provided a complete mechanism for its investigation, attachment and forfeiture of property, opportunity of hearing, appellate scrutiny and eventual prosecution, while expressly dispensing with prior conviction for the predicate offence as a prerequisite for proving money laundering. In this statutory setting, the proceedings under AMLA cannot be treated merely as an extension of the assessment and recovery machinery under the Ordinance, 2001, rather, they operate within their own statutory field. A similar approach is discernible from the United Kingdom regime under the Proceeds of Crime Act, 2002 (“POCA”). Sections 327 to 329 thereof deal with money-laundering offences, whereas Section 340 operates on an all-crimes basis; thus, proceeds arising from tax evasion are not excluded merely because the underlying activity otherwise concerns legitimate trade or income. In R v. The comparative significance of this reasoning, for the present purposes, lies in the distinction between determination of civil tax liability and criminal investigation into the character and subsequent dealing of property alleged to constitute proceeds of crime. The same approach was subsequently applied where cash was intercepted without identification of a particular predicate offence, while it was also recognized that proof of a specific type of underlying criminal conduct is not invariably necessary. These authorities, though persuasive, lend comparative support to the statutory scheme embodied in Explanation-II to Section 3 of AMLA, under which conviction for the respective predicate offence is expressly not required for proving the offence of money laundering. Thus, it is reinforced that the distinction between the existence and proof of criminal origin of the alleged proceeds, which remains essential and the requirement of obtaining a prior conviction or final civil tax assessment, is not required .

Bare perusal of Section 3 read with Explanation-II of AMLA clearly brings home the explicit statutory authority, thus, the legal framework separates the standalone crime of money laundering from the underlying criminal act which allegedly generates the illicit money because they are two distinct offences, money laundering and the predicate offence are tried independently or concurrently, consequently the outcome does not automatically bind the other. Likewise, the initiation and prosecution of the proceedings under AMLA cannot be directly pinned to the determination of tax liability under the provisions contained in the Ordinance, 2001. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has held in the case of Justice Qazi Faez Issa that the commission of a scheduled predicate offence is a sine qua non for money laundering. It is held that if there is no underlying crime, there are no proceeds of crime to launder, however, the Supreme Court of Pakistan separates the occurrence of the crime from a formal judicial conviction of that crime.

Another important statutory underpinning is that the relevant provisions under the Ordinance, 2001 i.e. Sections 192, 192A, 194, 199 have been inserted in Schedule-I to AMLA as per the mandate and authority conferred by the legislature by virtue of amendment/insertion of the relevant subject matter in Section-XII-A of the Schedule-I in terms of Section 42, read with clause (xxvi) of Section 2 of AMLA. By virtue of such inclusion, the aforesaid sections have been added in the definition of predicate offence, thus, the same cannot be rendered ineffective by importing into AMLA a condition precedent which its text does not expressly prescribes. 21. The apprehension that such investigation leaves a person without protection is also not borne out from the statutory scheme. Before proceeding to dilate upon this particular question, we want to record a specific statement made by the authorized officers of the respondent Department in presence of learned counsel for the respondent, who affirmed the same during the course of hearing that the respondents have throughout acted with restraint and will continue to abide by that arrangement as the respondents do not intend to arrest the petitioners, however, such a course and statement is conditional upon the petitioners joining the investigation. Sections 8 and 9 of AMLA regulate attachment and the consequential proceedings concerning property alleged to constitute proceeds of crime, while Section 23 of AMLA also provides a statutory appellate remedy before the High Court. The existence of such safeguards assumes importance while considering the argument that the entire statutory process be terminated at its inception through invocation of Constitutional jurisdiction.

22. The commission of a predicate offence is undoubtedly foundational to proceedings under AMLA as the proceeds of crime must necessarily trace their origin to such offence, nonetheless, it is distinct from requiring the entire civil or fiscal adjudicatory process concerning the predicate offence to first attain finality before the investigating agency may even inquire into the offence of money laundering. Whether a person is in possession of property derived from or representing proceeds of crime is essentially a question of fact to be determined on the basis of material collected during investigation. The statutory requirement of existence of a predicate offence, therefore, cannot be stretched to mean that investigation into the independent offence of money laundering must invariably remain in abeyance until culmination of all proceedings relating to the predicate offence. In this regard, we have considered the judgment handed down by the learned Single Judge in Chambers of this Court in Abdul Saboor’s case and are of the opinion that the findings rendered therein are in consonance with the settled principles of law and are based on true appreciation of the statutory scheme envisaged in AMLA and the Ordinance, 2001.

It is in the fitness of things to deal with the objection raised by the Petitioners regarding the use of expressions such as “Police Station”, “Police Officer”, “Investigating Officer” and “Complaint”, by borrowing their meaning from Cr.P.C. or another enactment. This submission has no lawful force without first examining the scheme in which those expressions have been employed. Clause (xviii) of Section 2 of AMLA defines ‘investigating Abdul Saboor v. Page 23 or prosecuting agency’, which includes DG I&I, similarly the offence of money laundering has been defined in Section 3 of AMLA. Under AMLA, the criminal prosecution for money laundering does not follow standard criminal procedure in isolation. Unlike the ordinary lodging of an FIR under section 154 of the Cr.P.C, investigation and prosecution under AMLA is rooted in separate process and steps before initiation of the process of prosecution; it involves the triggering phase of intelligence and report by means of STRs at the outset, generated by Financial Institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions, which monitor transactions and if a red flag is raised regarding the illicit origin of the asset a Cash Threshold Report (CTR) or STR, as the case may be, is generated. The STR is then routed to FMU, which analyzes the case. It is of note that the procedure and manner of furnishing information by reporting entities is regulated in terms of the provisions contained in Section 7 and Section 7-A to 7-J, of AMLA and no unbridled, unchecked or unregulated use of authority and domain of exercise of discretion is available, rather the same is confined within the statutory contours and conspicuous checks and balances. Learned counsel for the respondents has placed on record the documents and information, which have not been refuted by way of calling the same in question. The information so supplied depicts that FMU, while exercising its jurisdiction under Section 6 of AMLA uses specialized software to trace the flow of funds and match names against master domestic profiles; following that, the process of compiling of financial intelligence is undertaken and only if the transaction in issue reflects an outright pattern of criminal concealment and layering, the FMU creates a file for further processing and thereafter if FMU determines that underlying transaction involves predicate offence of money laundering and proceeds of crime are prima facie involved, the matter is forwarded to DG I&I. Once the DG I&I receives the report, the assigned Investigating Officer issues notices to the accused to explain the source of detected assets/funds/property; if no explanation is rendered or the explanation provided is unsatisfactory, the inquiry formally evolves into a full scale AMLA Investigation as it shifts from an intelligence handling process to a formal statutory criminal inquiry, Thus, the element of W.P. No. 2928 of 2026. Page 24 mala fide is relatively minimal if not absent in such cases. The first adverse action against an accused is contemplated under Section 8 of AMLA, whereby, an order of attachment of property may be passed but this authority is also circumscribed by definite statutory safeguards and intervention/permission by the Court. Therefore, we have no hesitation to hold on the basis of well settled principle of law that a statutory expression derives its content from the enactment in which it occurs, its context and the object sought to be achieved. A definition appearing in another statute cannot ordinarily be imported for interpreting an expression in the statute under consideration unless the enactments are pari materia; where the word is undefined, its meaning has to be gathered from its ordinary meaning read in the relevant statutory context . The same word may carry different meanings under different enactments and a meaning judicially assigned to an expression for purposes of one statutory scheme cannot necessarily be transplanted into another where doing so would disturb the latter's scheme and object . The objection founded merely upon terminology used in the general criminal law, therefore, cannot override the mechanism specifically created by AMLA. Comparative analysis may also be drawn from the Indian jurisdiction, where the Supreme Court of India, while examining the Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (“PMLA”) in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary’s case, treated the legislation as a special and self-contained statutory regime whose prescribed procedure prevails over the general procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure. It was further recognized that officers exercising investigative powers under the PMLA are not police officers undertaking an ordinary investigation under the general criminal law; consequently, absence of the conventional FIR mechanism does not prevent proceedings by the designated agency under the special enactment.

Consequently, the procedure expressly contemplated by AMLA cannot be displaced merely by invoking a different procedure available under the general criminal law i.e. Cr.P.C. or the taxing statute under Ordinance, 2001. DG I&I is the investigating and prosecuting agency under AMLA for the purpose of investigating the offence of money laundering, it has the necessary expertise to investigate the matter underlying the offence of money laundering. The offence of money laundering is inextricably linked to and dependent upon the predicate offence, therefore, any investigation must necessarily be conducted in respect of the latter by the Investigation Officer under AMLA.

25. The distinction assumes greater significance when the scheme of AMLA is examined in the context that AMLA is a special law enacted subsequent in time to the Ordinance, 2001, specifically to criminalize money laundering and to provide a mechanism concerning proceeds of crime. It is well settled that a subsequent special enactment operates according to its own legislative fiat and provisions of an earlier law cannot be stretched to defeat the same . The object of AMLA is materially different from the mere assessment or recovery of tax and is specifically directed towards prevention of money laundering, the attachment and confiscation of property generated from proceeds of crime having its genesis in a predicate offence . It is a well settled principle of interpretation of statute that a special law cannot be made dependent on a general law for its application. The principle of primacy of special law denotes that when a matter is governed by a targeted, special law and a broad general law, the special law operates as a complete and self-contained code for that specific subject and takes precedence. Similarly, the legal canon of anti-frustration logic requires that a special law may not be rendered dependent on the application of general law. To allow a general law or its provisions to dictate the terms, timings or validity of a special law, degrades the clarity of the special statute and results in judicial Gulistan Textile Mills Ltd. v. The test of frustration requires that the Courts must resist reading general law in a manner that “throttles the special law”. The core legal doctrine which needs to be considered is that if the application of the special law is made contingent upon conditions outlined in a general law, the very purpose of creating a distinct, specialized legal mechanism is defeated.

When a special enactment is passed by the legislature, it represents the absolute will of the legislature regarding that exact topic and if an interpreter seeks to create “chain of dependency” where the special law cannot move until a general law term is applied, it creates a logical fallacy, thus, if the legislature wanted the general law to dictate terms, it would not have bothered to draft a separate, distinct special enactment.

We are of the considered opinion that the clear intent of the legislature, which arises out of the purpose, scope and provisions of AMLA provides prevention of money laundering and not to enforce the tax statutes.

26. To examine the plea of quashment of FIRs, the grounds have to be appreciated within the settled contours of jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution. There is no cavil with the proposition that registration of an FIR and conduct of investigation are amenable to judicial review and may be declared without lawful authority where the jurisdictional prerequisites for such interference are unquestionably established.

However, amenability to judicial review is altogether different from substituting constitutional jurisdiction for the statutory process of investigation and trial. This Court, while exercising Constitutional jurisdiction cannot assume the role of an investigating agency and quash FIR, save in very exceptional circumstances.

It is well settled by now that short-circuiting the normal procedure prescribed by law through exercise of equitable jurisdiction is impermissible. The foregoing principle gains an overarching force where the controversy requires investigation into disputed facts and evaluation of evidentiary material. Adverting to the principal reliance of the petitioners upon the landmark judgment of Taj International supra , the said judgment arose within the statutory scheme of the Sales Tax Act, 1990. Respectfully, its reasoning is linked to the scheme governing assessment, determination of tax liability and initiation of criminal proceedings under that enactment at the relevant time. On the contrary, AMLA neither constitutes the machinery for assessment of sales tax or income tax nor makes prosecution for money laundering merely another mode for recovery of such tax. It creates an independent offence directed towards proceeds of crime and their subsequent dealing in the manner contemplated by a special law. More importantly, the statutory provision considered in Taj International supra, particularly Section 37A of the Sales Tax Act, 1990, has subsequently undergone changes by virtue of amendments therein. Respectfully, a judgment cannot be generalized beyond its context, as it is only applicable to the situation at hand and does not serve as a precedent for matters that lie outside its explicit scope. This principle underscores the limited applicability of judgments and reinforces the need for careful analysis when considering their implications in future cases . The ratio of a judgment rendered upon a statutory provision is to be understood with reference to the text of the law interpreted therein; where the legislature subsequently alters the material statutory scheme, the earlier interpretation, with respect and reverence, cannot be extended to proceedings governed by the amended provision, much less transplanted wholesomely into another special enactment having different genesis, object, ingredients, procedure and remedies. In view of the above reasoning that AMLA being a special enactment cannot be rendered dependent upon the provisions of the Ordinance, 2001, the ratio decidendi of Taj International is not attracted in the case in hand as it is well settled that a case is only authority for what it actually decides and cannot be cited as precedent for a proposition that may be inferred from it.
